981.title: The Ottomans rise
981.hook: a small Anatolian state becomes an empire
981.howItsDone: Turkish Muslims visit the tombs of Osman and Orhan in Bursa, and the story of Osman's dream is still told as the founding legend of the Ottoman dynasty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Seljuks, and the stone road houses they built for travelers. Your line was: the road houses. Who did you give a moment of rest? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

When the Seljuk sultans of Anatolia weakened, their land broke into small principalities, each with its own chief, its own few towns, its own horsemen. On the far northwest edge, facing the Byzantine Empire, sat a small one. A frontier strip of hills and pasture. Its leader was a man named Osman. Seen from the old Seljuk city of Konya, he was one frontier chief among several. And yet his name would one day be carried by a great empire. In English, Osman's people became the Ottomans. Today: the Ottomans rise.
screen: `THE SELJUK LANDS BREAK APART.` → `A SMALL STATE ON THE EDGE.` → `A MAN NAMED OSMAN.`

segments.voice: Later Ottoman chroniclers tell a story about Osman's beginnings. It's a story people tell, not a record. Osman is staying in the house of a holy man, a sheikh. He falls asleep and dreams that a moon rises from the sheikh's chest and settles into his own. Then a tree grows from him, and its branches spread until their shade covers mountains, rivers and cities. When he wakes, the sheikh reads the dream as a promise for his descendants, and gives Osman his daughter in marriage. Whatever happened in that house, the story tells you how the dynasty wanted to be remembered: blessed by a man of God, from a seed that grew. The real growth was slower and more ordinary. Osman and his son Orhan took towns one at a time from the Byzantines. Orhan made Bursa their city, and father and son are buried there. They drew in warriors, scholars, Sufi brotherhoods and Christian villagers alike. Step by step, one town, then a region, then a crossing into Europe. A small frontier state became an empire. The Qur'an has a line about small things that matter. In Pickthall's translation: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then." And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, holds that the deeds God loves best are those done steadily, even if they are small. An empire is not a good deed, and the Ottomans did both good and harm. But the shape of the story is worth keeping: a seed, a dream, and a lot of patient steps. From small beginnings.
screen: `A SHEIKH'S HOUSE, A DREAM.` · `A TREE WHOSE SHADE COVERS CITIES.` · `ONE TOWN AT A TIME: BURSA.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD.` · then, large: `FROM SMALL BEGINNINGS.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about small beginnings. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing in your life that started small: a friendship that began with one conversation, a skill that began with one clumsy try, a habit of prayer or kindness that began on one ordinary day. Hold it for a while. Then think of one small seed you could plant today, so small it feels almost silly. If you pray, you can ask for it to grow. If you don't, simply choose it. The bell holds the time.
Osman. The frontier chief whose small state in Anatolia grew one town at a time into the Ottoman empire. Today's word.
Your line: from small beginnings. Today, plant one small seed: a first page, a first call, a first step, and don't judge it by its size. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

982.title: Constantinople, 1453
982.hook: Mehmed II takes Constantinople, which becomes Istanbul
982.howItsDone: The conquest is commemorated in Istanbul, while Orthodox Christians remember the same event as the fall of the city; the Ecumenical Patriarchate still has its seat there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ottomans rise: Osman's small frontier state, growing one town at a time. Your line was: from small beginnings. What seed did you plant? Day nine hundred eighty-two.

Ships are moving over a hill. Not sailing around it. Over it. Oxen strain at ropes, men push from behind, and wooden warships slide across greased timbers laid on the ground, up the slope and down the other side, into a harbor that a great iron chain was supposed to keep closed. Inside the walls, the defenders wake to find enemy ships on water they thought was safe. The city is Constantinople, the old capital of the Byzantine emperors. The man who ordered the ships over the hill is a young Ottoman sultan named Mehmed. Today's word: Constantinople.
screen: `SHIPS MOVING OVER A HILL.` → `A HARBOR CLOSED BY A CHAIN.` → `A YOUNG SULTAN NAMED MEHMED.`

segments.voice: Constantinople sat where Europe meets Asia, on a narrow strait called the Bosphorus, with the Golden Horn harbor on one side. Its land walls had turned back earlier armies, including Muslim ones. The city had also been in Muslim imaginations for a long time. A saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, praises the commander and the army who will one day take Constantinople. Scholars have debated how strong that saying's chain of narrators is, but the Ottomans took it to heart. Mehmed prepared like a builder. He raised a fortress on the European shore of the Bosphorus to control the strait. He brought great cannons to batter the walls. When the chain kept his fleet out of the harbor, he moved the ships overland. After a long siege, the walls were breached. The last Byzantine emperor died in the fighting. And then came days that need to be told honestly: the city was plundered, and people were killed or carried off into captivity. Conquest in that age was cruel, and Orthodox Christians still remember the day as the fall of the city. Then Mehmed set about refilling the city. He brought in Muslims, Christians and Jews from across his lands, and made it his capital. In time, the name Istanbul took hold, though Ottoman documents went on using forms of the old name too. For Muslims it became the seat of an empire; for Orthodox Christians, it remains the city of their ancient patriarch. One city, carrying both. Istanbul.

Constantinople. The Byzantine capital on the Bosphorus, taken by Mehmed after a long siege, and in time called Istanbul. Today's word.
Your line: istanbul. Today, when you see a place with two names, ask who calls it what, and why both names matter to someone. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: Hagia Sophia
983.hook: the church becomes a mosque, then a museum, then a mosque again, felt deeply by both faiths
983.howItsDone: Hagia Sophia is used today as a mosque for the five daily prayers and Friday prayer, and it stays open to visitors of every faith outside prayer times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople: ships over a hill, a long siege, and a city with two names. Your line was: istanbul. Where did you notice a place with two names? Day nine hundred eighty-three.

Step inside and look up. A dome so wide and so high it seems to float, held up, as an old description put it, as if hung from heaven by a chain. A ring of windows runs around its base, so the light pours in just under the curve. Up on the walls, faces in gold mosaic: Mary, Christ, emperors. Across from them, huge round panels in Arabic calligraphy, bearing the names of God, the Prophet and those close to him. Both are there, in the same air. One building, loved by people who pray in very different ways. Today: Hagia Sophia.
screen: `A DOME THAT SEEMS TO FLOAT.` → `GOLD MOSAICS: MARY AND CHRIST.` → `ROUND PANELS: THE NAMES OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Hagia Sophia is Greek for Holy Wisdom. It was built by the Byzantine emperor Justinian as the great church of Constantinople, where emperors were crowned and the liturgy was sung beneath that dome. When Mehmed took the city, he went to Hagia Sophia, and it became a mosque. Friday prayer was held there. Minarets rose at its corners. A mihrab was set in the wall to face Mecca, a little off the line of the old church. Over time, the Christian images were covered over, and the great calligraphy panels were hung. For Ottoman Muslims, it became a sign that God had given them the city. For Orthodox Christians, its loss became a lasting grief. Much later, the Turkish Republic made it a museum. The plaster came off some mosaics, and visitors of every faith walked in to look up. And in recent years, it was made a mosque again. Some Muslims celebrated. Some Christians, and others, grieved. Today it is open to visitors outside prayer times, and the Christian images are veiled while prayer is held. The Qur'an speaks of houses of worship of more than one faith in the same breath. Among the places that would have been pulled down had God not held some people back by others, it names, in Pickthall's translation, "cloisters and churches and oratories and mosques, wherein the name of Allah is oft mentioned". Commentators differ over whether that last phrase means all four, or the mosques alone. This lesson doesn't settle the argument. It asks only that both griefs and both joys be heard. A building many love.
screen: `HOLY WISDOM: A GREAT CHURCH.` · `A MOSQUE: MINARETS AND A MIHRAB.` · `A MUSEUM, THEN A MOSQUE AGAIN.` · `CHURCHES AND MOSQUES IN ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `A BUILDING MANY LOVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: respect between faiths. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the dome, the gold faces and the great round names, all under the same light. Then think of someone whose faith or tradition is not your own, and who loves a place or a practice that you love too, or that you share a city with. Picture them standing next to you under that dome. If you pray, you can ask, in your own words, for respect between faiths. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Hagia Sophia. Holy Wisdom: a great church, then a mosque, then a museum, and a mosque again, loved and grieved by Christians and Muslims alike. Today's word.
Your line: a building many love. Today, when you hear an argument over a holy place, listen once for what each side loves before you take a side. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Suleyman the Lawgiver
984.hook: the sultan remembered in Turkey for law and justice
984.howItsDone: In Turkey, Suleyman is known as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, and Muslim scholars still distinguish between the sharia and the laws a ruler issues on matters the sharia leaves open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hagia Sophia: Holy Wisdom, a church, a mosque, a museum and a mosque again. Your line was: a building many love. Did you hear what each side loves? Day nine hundred eighty-four.

One sultan, two nicknames. In Europe he's called Suleyman the Magnificent, for the splendor of his court, his armies at the gates of Vienna, his fleets on the Mediterranean. But in Turkey, people remember him by a different name, a quieter one: Kanuni. The lawgiver. Not the conqueror. Not the magnificent. The man who wrote things down so that people would know what the rules were. What a ruler is remembered for at home can be very different from what neighbors notice. Today: Suleyman the Lawgiver.
screen: `ONE SULTAN, TWO NICKNAMES.` → `THE MAGNIFICENT, IN EUROPE.` → `KANUNI, AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Kanun means law, and specifically the law a ruler issues. In the Ottoman Empire there were two streams of law flowing side by side. One was the sharia, God's law as worked out by Muslim scholars from the Qur'an and the example of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The sultan could not change it. The other was kanun: the ruler's decrees on things the sharia left open, like land, taxes, the ranks of officials, the duties of provinces. Suleyman's reign is remembered for gathering and organizing these decrees, so that a judge in a distant town and a peasant on his land could, at least in principle, know what was owed and what was fair. Beside him stood the chief mufti, the scholar Ebussuud Efendi, who worked to show how the sultan's law fit within the sharia. Justice was the point. The Qur'an asks believers to hold to it even when it costs them. In Pickthall's translation: "Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves." Suleyman wasn't only a lawmaker. He wrote poetry under a pen name, Muhibbi, the loving one. And his reign had its darkness too: he ordered the death of one of his own sons. A lawgiver is not a saint, and the tradition remembers both. Still, the name that stuck at home is this one. Not the size of the empire. The fairness of its rules. The lawgiver.
screen: `TWO STREAMS: SHARIA AND KANUN.` · `THE RULER'S LAW, WRITTEN DOWN.` · `STAUNCH IN JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOURSELF.` · `A POET, AND A FATHER'S DARKNESS.` · then, large: `THE LAWGIVER.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep one rule fairly. Settle, and breathe. Think of a rule you're in charge of: at home, at work, in a team, with your kids, with yourself. Bedtime. Screen time. Who does the dishes. Who gets the last word in a meeting. Ask one honest question: do I keep this rule the same for everyone, including me? Pick one rule to keep evenly today, even against yourself. If you pray, you can ask for a fair heart. If you don't, simply pick the rule. The bell holds the time.
Kanun. The ruler's law that Suleyman, Kanuni the lawgiver, organized beside the sharia, in the name of justice. Today's word.
Your line: the lawgiver. Today, keep one rule fairly, the same for everyone, and notice if it costs you. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: Sinan the architect
985.hook: the architect of a great many buildings, including the Suleymaniye
985.howItsDone: Sinan's mosques, including the Suleymaniye in Istanbul and the Selimiye in Edirne, are still used for daily and Friday prayers, with worshipers in rows under their domes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suleyman the Lawgiver: kanun beside the sharia, and justice even against yourself. Your line was: the lawgiver. Which rule did you keep fairly? Day nine hundred eighty-five.

On a hill above the Golden Horn in Istanbul stands a great mosque with four minarets, and around it, a whole small town: schools, a hospital, a kitchen that fed the poor, a bathhouse, shops. Behind the mosque, in a garden, lies the tomb of the sultan who paid for it, Suleyman. And just outside the complex, at a street corner, there's another tomb, much smaller, plain and simple. It belongs to the man who designed all of it. He rests near the sultan he served, but not inside. Today: Sinan the architect.
screen: `A MOSQUE AND A SMALL TOWN AROUND IT.` → `THE SULTAN'S TOMB IN THE GARDEN.` → `A SMALL TOMB AT THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sinan did not start as an architect. By his own account, given to a friend who wrote it down, he was taken as a young man into the sultan's service and became a soldier. On campaign, he built bridges and boats for the army. Engineering under pressure, with rivers to cross and no time to waste. Only later was he made chief architect of the empire, and from then on, mosques, schools, bridges, bathhouses, fountains and kitchens came off his drawing board across the Ottoman lands. Tradition credits him with a great many buildings. The Suleymaniye, the complex on that hill, was built for Suleyman. Sinan himself, in his memoirs, sorted three of his mosques like stages in a craftsman's life: an early one in Istanbul as his apprentice work, the Suleymaniye as the work of a journeyman, and the Selimiye in Edirne as his masterpiece. What was he chasing? Space and light. Under his great domes, the room opens out so there's little in the way, and windows set high and low let the light fall evenly across the floor. Muslims gather in rows on one carpet, shoulder to shoulder, facing Mecca, and Sinan's domes give those rows a single, unbroken sky. The Qur'an's verse of light comes to mind in rooms like these. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." A dome doesn't explain that verse. But it can make a crowd go quiet. The architect.

segments.voice: The practice: look at a dome. If you're near one, a mosque, a church, a station, a planetarium, go and look up. If not, search for a photo of the inside of the Suleymaniye's dome, or simply look up at whatever ceiling is above you right now. Settle, and breathe. Notice where the light comes from. Notice how the shape gathers your eyes upward. If you pray, you can let the looking become prayer. If you don't, let it simply be looking. The bell holds the time.
Sinan. The soldier-engineer who became the Ottoman chief architect, designed the Suleymaniye, and filled his domes with light. Today's word.
Your line: the architect. Today, look up inside one building you use every day, and notice where its light comes from. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: Communities in the empire
986.hook: Christians and Jews run their own community affairs under Ottoman rule
986.howItsDone: In Turkey today, the Greek Orthodox and Armenian patriarchates and a chief rabbinate still have their seats in Istanbul, a living trace of the Ottoman community arrangements.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sinan the architect, the soldier who built bridges and then domes full of light. Your line was: the architect. What did you notice when you looked up? Day nine hundred eighty-six.

A wedding in an Ottoman city. The bride and groom are Armenian Christians, and the priest who marries them answers to the Armenian patriarch, not to the local Muslim judge. Down the street, a Jewish family settles an inheritance before a rabbinic court. Across town, Greek Orthodox children learn their letters in a school run by their own church. And in the great mosque, Muslims gather for Friday prayer. All of them live under one sultan. Each group handles much of its own life by its own rules. Today's word names that arrangement: millet.
screen: `AN ARMENIAN WEDDING.` → `A RABBINIC COURT.` → `A GREEK CHURCH SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an has a word for a religion, a way of faith: milla. It speaks of the milla of Abraham, in Pickthall's translation, "the religion of Abraham, the upright." In the Ottoman Empire, the word millet came to mean a religious community, with its own leaders and its own law for many of life's matters. After taking Constantinople, Mehmed saw to it that the Greek Orthodox Church had a patriarch again, and gave him authority over his flock. Armenian Christians had their patriarch. Jews had their rabbis and, in time, a chief rabbi. Inside each community, marriage, divorce, inheritance, worship, schools and charity were largely run by its own leaders, by its own law. Some readers bring a verse to mind here. Pickthall renders it: "For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way." Now the honest part, because this was not equality. Christians and Jews were protected subjects, dhimmis. They paid a special tax, the jizya, and lived under limits that Muslims did not. Muslims held the highest offices. Some periods and places were generous; others were harsh. And historians today debate how much of a formal system there was before the empire's last century, or whether the word was used for older, looser arrangements. Still, for a long time, different peoples of faith lived side by side in the same cities, each keeping its own feasts, its own courts, its own way of marrying and burying. Each its own community.
screen: `MILLA: A WAY OF FAITH.` · `A PATRIARCH, A RABBI, THEIR OWN COURTS.` · `PROTECTED, BUT NOT EQUAL.` · `HISTORIANS STILL DEBATE THE SYSTEM.` · then, large: `EACH ITS OWN COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: respect a community's own ways. Settle, and breathe. Think of a community near you whose ways are not yours: a church, a synagogue, a mosque, a temple, a gurdwara, or simply a neighborhood with customs you don't share. Bring to mind one thing they do that you don't fully understand: a fast, a holiday, a way of dressing, a way of mourning. Let yourself be curious about it. What does it protect for them? 987.title: The Safavids
987.hook: a Sufi family from Ardabil takes a throne, and Twelver Shi'ism becomes the faith of Iran
987.howItsDone: Shi'a Muslims in Iran and beyond make pilgrimage to the shrines of the Imams and their families, such as Imam Reza in Mashhad and Fatima Masuma in Qom, to pray, read and remember them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the millet: Christians and Jews in the Ottoman lands running their own community affairs. Your line was: each its own community. What did you learn about how a neighboring community celebrates or mourns? Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

In the city of Mashhad, in the northeast of Iran, a golden dome rises over a grave. Day and night, people come: pilgrims with bags from long bus rides, students, grandmothers, families with small children asleep on their shoulders. They touch the lattice around the tomb, they pray, they weep, they sit on the carpets in the courtyards and talk. The man buried there is Imam Reza, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. For Shi'a Muslims he is one of the Imams, the rightful guides of the community. Iran had not always been a Shi'a land. Today, the family that made it one. The Safavids.

segments.voice: The Safavids began not as kings but as a Sufi order, led by a family of sheikhs in the town of Ardabil, in the northwest of Iran. Their followers were devoted, Turkish-speaking horsemen among them who wore a red cap and were called the Qizilbash, the red heads. Out of that order came a young leader named Isma'il, who took the old Persian title of shah and won a kingdom. And he made one choice that shaped Iran from then on: Twelver Shi'ism would be the faith of the state. Twelver Shi'a Muslims hold that leadership after the Prophet belonged to his family, beginning with his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and passing through a line of Imams, the last of whom is in hiding and will return. Sunni Muslims hold that the community rightly chose its leaders, the caliphs. Both read the same Qur'an. One verse shows how a single line can be heard two ways. The Prophet is told to say that he asks no payment for his message, only love for those near of kin. Shi'a commentators hear the Prophet's family in it; Sunni commentators have also read it in other ways. The Safavid change was not gentle everywhere. Scholars were brought in, Sunni practice was pushed out, and Iran grew apart from its Ottoman neighbors, who were Sunni and often at war with the shahs. The shrines grew in honor: Imam Reza in Mashhad, his sister Fatima Masuma in Qom. A whole country's map of pilgrimage was redrawn. Iran becomes Shia.

segments.voice: The practice: learn about Iran's shrines, in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the courtyard in Mashhad: the carpets, the families, the gold dome. Now think about a place where people you love are buried, or a place you go back to when you need to remember who you belong to. What do people do there? What do they bring? Afterward, if you have a few minutes, look up a picture of the shrine of Imam Reza or of Fatima Masuma in Qom. If you pray, you can pray for the people who travel there. If you don't, simply hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
